                                  Summary of Argument
        Route 894 remains the route that best satisﬁes PURA §37.056(c) and 16 TAC
§25.101(b)(3)(B). It is the Joint Applicants’ best-meets route and Brian C. Andrews’s
independent recommendation. It avoids Links E6 and E12, the two link-level habitable-
structure outliers; has 85 habitable structures, the fewest among the principal routes of
interest; places no right-of-way within the Environmental Assessment’s standardized
park foreground-visual-zone metric; and occupies the strongest cost-versus-habitable-
structure position in the ﬁled-route data. 1
        The initial briefs do not supply a route-wide reason to displace Route 894.
They divide into several camps. The Joint Applicants and many intervenors support
Route 894. Commission Staﬀ and several other parties support Route 487. Some parties
advocate Routes 296, 572, Cherokee Creek G, Route 894 Western Modiﬁcation 1,
or custom routes. A smaller northern-corridor group advances Route 392, Route 410,
or a broader slate of northern routes. Within that group, the Mewhinney Family, Brady
Creek Intervenors, and Solana Intervenors aﬃrmatively request Route 392; Staten Creek
Ranch identiﬁes Routes 392 and 410 as attractive northern alternatives; 4K Land and
Cattle includes them within a much broader northern-corridor slate; and the K13/K51
Landowners oﬀer Routes 392 and 410 only as fallbacks behind southern routes. 2 Whitis
requests Whitis 1-14 and uses Route 392 principally to attack the weighing of habitable
structures and compatible right-of-way. 3

transmission corridor should control the route decision. That premise confuses

                                            Argument
                                      I. Introduction

        This Reply Brief does not rebrief uncontested issues or respond to every ﬁling
merely because a party ﬁled a brief. The initial briefs reﬂect hundreds of legitimate
property-speciﬁc, link-speciﬁc, route-speciﬁc, environmental, cultural, and community
concerns. They also conﬁrm why the Commission cannot select a route by counting
briefs or by treating the avoidance of any one property as the route-selection test.
        The routing question is whether the whole record supports displacing Route 894,
the route selected by the Joint Applicants and independently recommended by Mr.
Andrews. It does not. The principal adverse briefs rest on six recurring arguments: (1)
U3 and hard-infrastructure paralleling should control; (2) the habitable-structure data
are inaccurate or over-weighted; (3) K2/K3, karst, and alleged cost-input uncertainty
undermine Route 894; (4) the one-half-mile foreground-zone metric understates park
impacts; (5) Applicants failed to capture the full status of Solana’s development; and
(6) Applicants’ qualitative balancing should be replaced with a separate scored or
geospatial methodology. Each identiﬁes a consideration the Commission may weigh.
None establishes that Route 392, Route 410, or any other proposed alternative performs
better than Route 894 on the complete route-level record.
        The Commission selects a route, not a crossing concept, a private composite
score, a parcel-protection agreement, or a tally of parties. Route 894 remains the route
with the best overall balance.

      III. Order of Referral and Preliminary Order Issues

       A. Application and Route Adequacy (Issue No. 1)

        Not addressed further. The route-adequacy disputes do not establish that any
northern-corridor route best satisﬁes the Commission’s route-selection criteria. All ﬁled
routes remain subject to the same route-wide comparison.

       B. Notice (Issue Nos. 2-3)

        Not addressed further. Several briefs describe late notice or the addition of links
after public meetings. Those concerns may inform the Commission’s evaluation of the
process and aﬀected landowners, but they do not supply a route-wide basis to reject
Route 894.

       C. Public Input (Issue No. 4) and Community Values

        The initial briefs show broad participation and no route-selection consensus.
Parties supporting Route 894, Route 487, Route 296, Route 572, Cherokee Creek G,
Route 392, Route 410, Whitis 1-14, and numerous other alternatives all identify sincere
harms to particular properties, resources, or communities. That pattern conﬁrms the
point made in Hodge-Schwertner Intervenors’ Initial Brief: public input identiﬁes
relevant concerns, but route-wide evidence decides the route. 11
        The Commission should therefore give community-values evidence its proper
weight without converting the number of ﬁlings or the intensity of a coalition’s
opposition into a controlling criterion. The Route 392 proponents’ concerns about
Solana Ranch, Brady Creek Ranch, Deep Creek Ranch, Staten Creek Ranch, and the
northern corridor are relevant. So are the existing homes, schools, creek corridors,
planned developments, working ranches, cultural resources, and long-standing land uses
aﬀected by E12 and the rest of Route 392. Selecting Route 392 would not eliminate
landowner and community impacts, but would only transfer and increase them.
        The aligned Save Our Salado (“SOS”) record, ﬁled by E12-area landowners with
limited-scope assistance from the undersigned counsel, helps make that transfer
concrete. It identiﬁes the Edwards bedrooms and patio 98 feet from the proposed E12
easement, the Morison home 185 feet away in a household with a pacemaker recipient,

SOS supports Route 894 or another route that avoids E12; it does not establish Route
894 over every other non-E12 route. But the evidence demonstrates that the harms
shifted onto E12 are existing and measurable, not abstract. Route 894 also avoids Link

defend Import Path 2. For route selection, however, the relevant point remains narrow:
even a ﬁnding of need does not privilege U3, Route 392, or any other route. Each route
must be evaluated under PURA §37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC §25.101(b)(3)(B). 13
